entries.clue: Gentlemanly monster, one giving way to everyone (7)

indicatorNotes.giving way to: To give way to somebody is to stand aside and let them have your place, so the letter named before it is lifted out and the piece named after it drops into the gap.

blocks.note: a giant is the monster of fairy tales
everyone is all of them
the Roman numeral for one, which is the letter standing in the middle of GIANT

annotation.surface: A monster with manners, stepping back so that the whole crowd can go first.
annotation.walkthrough: I is the only letter of GIANT that can be read as a number, which is what makes the swap fair. Pasquale writes it as an act of courtesy, so the wordplay and the definition describe the same gesture.
annotation.definitionFit: A gallant man is attentive and courteous towards others, the old chivalric sense of the word that 'gentlemanly' still carries.

entries.clue: Composer full of love, repeatedly kind, ultimately gives encouraging words (4,4)

indicatorNotes.full of: Something full of a thing has it inside, so the letters named next are packed into the middle of the word before.
indicatorNotes.ultimately: Ultimately means at the very end, so only the final letter of the word in front of it is taken.

blocks.note: Christoph Willibald Gluck, the eighteenth-century opera composer, whose name parts after its first letter to take a filling
love is a score of nothing at tennis, written as O, and it is wanted twice over
the last letter of kind

annotation.surface: A composer who is soppy and kind by turns, sending somebody off with warm words.
annotation.walkthrough: Gluck is the name to bank: five letters that open after the G and swallow three more. Love for O comes from the tennis scoreboard, where a score of nothing has been called love since the game was French.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Good luck' is the set phrase you say to somebody about to attempt something difficult, so it is encouragement itself rather than a synonym for the idea.

entries.clue: See 1
Generally inadequate, ill? Avoid this harmful substance (8)

indicatorNotes.inadequate: Something inadequate falls short of what it should be, so the word in front of it is left one letter shy of its full length.
indicatorNotes.ill: An ill person is out of sorts, and letters out of sorts are letters out of the order they were given in.

blocks.note: GENERALLY docked of its final Y, leaving eight letters to shuffle

annotation.surface: A warning to anybody who is below par and off colour about what to keep away from.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Inadequate' and 'ill' look like one complaint and are two separate instructions, the first shortening the word and the second disturbing it. An allergen is harmless to most people and dangerous only to those sensitive to it.
annotation.definitionFit: An allergen is a substance — pollen, peanuts, dust — that sets off an allergic reaction, so it does real harm to anyone susceptible.

entries.clue: Carried child on to bed – beginning to drift off (5)

indicatorNotes.beginning to drift off: What drifts off goes away, and here it is the beginning that does the drifting, so the first letter of the word before it never arrives.

blocks.note: a tot is a small child
BED with its opening B gone

annotation.surface: Lifting a small child onto the bed just as they start to fall asleep.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to drift off' is the sleepy half of the picture and a beheading instruction underneath, and that double duty is the whole of the difficulty. Tote is chiefly American — the tote bag is the one you carry.
annotation.definitionFit: To tote something is to lug or carry it about, and the past tense sits exactly where 'Carried' does.

entries.clue: Caress female individual endlessly led astray (6)

indicatorNotes.endlessly: Endlessly means without an end, so the word it follows gives up its final letter.
indicatorNotes.astray: Letters led astray have wandered off the path they were set in, so they arrive in a different order.

blocks.note: f is the standard abbreviation for female, as on a form
an individual is ONE, here with its last letter gone
the three letters of LED rearranged

annotation.surface: A woman on her own being taken in, over and over, by somebody with designs on her.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Led astray' does two jobs at once: it is the seduction the surface describes and the shuffle the parse needs. Only three letters are in that shuffle, which is why the instruction is so easy to miss.
annotation.definitionFit: To fondle is to stroke or handle affectionately, which is what a caress amounts to.

entries.clue: Greek characters in ‘ouse maybe chatter (6)

indicatorNotes.maybe: 'Maybe' warns that the thing named is only one example of what is wanted, so the word to use is the broader one it belongs to.

blocks.note: a house is one sort of home, and the dropped aitch the clue has already written carries straight over into 'ome
to gas is to talk on and on about nothing much

annotation.surface: Idle gossip going on inside what might well be a house.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is the setter telling you the aitch has gone already, so the only move left is from house to home. Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, the one in 'alpha and omega'.
annotation.definitionFit: Omega is a letter of the Greek alphabet, so the plural answers 'Greek characters' as a plain synonym.

entries.clue: Vile celebs paid off (10)

indicatorNotes.off: Something that has gone off has turned bad and no longer holds its proper shape, so the letters in front of it are rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

annotation.surface: Famous names taking money to keep something quiet.
annotation.walkthrough: Three words of clue, and the shuffle rests on 'off' alone — the sense in which milk goes off, not the sense in which a debt is settled. The fodder is exactly the length of the answer, which is the one clue to the mechanism.
annotation.definitionFit: Despicable means deserving contempt, which is the judgement 'vile' passes.

entries.clue: Praising group of countries concerned with activity of shifting goods? (10)

blocks.note: the European Union, a bloc of member states, is EU

blocks.clueFragment: concerned with activity of shifting goods
blocks.note: logistics is the business of moving goods about, and logistic is its adjective

annotation.surface: A trade bloc taking an interest in how freight gets moved around.
annotation.walkthrough: Two halves set side by side with no indicator and no link word between them, which is the plainest shape a charade can take. Eulogistic comes from eulogy, the speech of praise delivered over the dead.
annotation.definitionFit: To be eulogistic is to speak in praise of somebody, so the adjective fills exactly the slot 'Praising' holds.

entries.clue: Old form of salute conveying cold kiss (8)

indicatorNotes.form of: Asking for a form of something asks for one of the arrangements its letters can take, not for the word as it stands.

blocks.note: o is the standard abbreviation for old
the letters of SALUTE with C, the abbreviation for cold, carried along among them

annotation.surface: A stiff outdated salute that conveys nothing but coldness.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Old' is an abbreviation rather than a comment on the salute, though the surface works hard to make you read it the other way. Osculate is the formal Latinate verb that dictionaries keep and nobody says aloud.
annotation.definitionFit: To osculate is to kiss, the mock-solemn verb a zoologist or a crossword uses where an ordinary speaker would not.

entries.clue: Gaining inner peace, wife left scoundrel (6)

indicatorNotes.Gaining inner: What is gained on the inside lands between the letters either side of it, so this piece goes in the middle rather than at either end.

blocks.note: w is the standard abbreviation for wife
ease is the untroubled state that peace of mind amounts to
l is the standard abbreviation for left

annotation.surface: Somebody who has found calm at last now that the wife has gone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Wife left' is one phrase on the surface and two unrelated abbreviations underneath, which is the hinge the clue turns on. A weasel is a person as much as an animal: slippery, evasive, not to be trusted.
annotation.definitionFit: To call a man a weasel is to call him sly and untrustworthy, which is what a scoundrel is.

entries.clue: Leader avoiding bike training called ‘old-fashioned’ (6)

indicatorNotes.Leader avoiding: The leader is the letter at the head of the word, and a leader that avoids the answer never gets into it.

blocks.note: a bike is a CYCLE, less the C leading it
PT is physical training, the British school timetable's name for gym and games
a warning about the answer rather than a piece of wordplay: the word wanted is an archaic one, and this phrase contributes no letters

annotation.surface: A boss who has been ducking out of cycling sessions and gets written off as behind the times.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks are Pasquale owning up: no living speaker uses this word, which survives only in deliberate mock-medieval writing. 'Leader' is a letter, not a person, and that is the step the surface hides best.
annotation.definitionFit: Yclept is the archaic past participle of clepe, to call, so it means named or called — 'a knight yclept Gawain'.

entries.clue: Going before GP, I need care sorted out – pills finally swallowed (12)

indicatorNotes.sorted out: To sort something out is to put it into a different arrangement, which is what happens to these letters.
indicatorNotes.swallowed: A swallowed pill disappears inside, so the letter it gives up joins the letters being rearranged instead of standing outside them.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters
the last letter of pills

annotation.surface: A patient rehearsing the complaint for the doctor and taking the last of the tablets.
annotation.walkthrough: 'GP' sits in plain sight as fodder rather than as the abbreviation every solver expects it to be. 'Going before' is the euphemism the undertaker and the doctor share, which is what makes the surface's waiting room quietly grim.
annotation.definitionFit: To predecease someone is to die before them, and 'going before' is the gentle idiom for dying, so both halves of the sense match.

entries.clue: Husband in conflict, having got caress from someone at quayside (10)

indicatorNotes.in: A thing put in another sits inside it, so the letter named first goes between the letters of the word named next.

blocks.note: war is armed conflict, and the word opens after its W
h is the standard abbreviation for husband, as on a family tree
to finger something is to run the fingers over it

annotation.surface: A husband caught up in a row who has been getting affectionate with somebody else.
annotation.walkthrough: A wharfinger is the keeper or owner of a wharf, the man answerable for everything landed on it. The word is Victorian commercial English and survives now mostly in shipping law.
annotation.definitionFit: A wharfinger owns or has charge of a wharf, so he is literally the someone standing at the quayside.

entries.clue: Sugary treat organised during affair (10)

indicatorNotes.organised: To organise something is to put it into a fresh arrangement, so the letters before this word are reordered.
indicatorNotes.during: What happens during something happens in the middle of it, so these letters drop inside the word named after.

blocks.note: a fling is a brief affair, and the word opens after its FL
the five letters of TREAT rearranged

annotation.surface: Somebody laying on a box of sweets in the middle of a love affair.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sugary treat' reads as one phrase and breaks straight down the middle, the first word the definition and the second the letters. Flattery earns 'sugary' because it is sweet and does the person who swallows it no good at all.
annotation.definitionFit: Sugary describes talk sweetened past the point of honesty, which is exactly the register of flattering praise.

entries.clue: The female’s embracing prince, having wasted time with princess and old guard? (10)

indicatorNotes.embracing: To embrace is to fold your arms right round something, so the word before it closes over everything named after.
indicatorNotes.having wasted: To waste a thing is to throw it away, so the letter named next is gone from the name it belonged to.

blocks.note: punctuation is never binding: 'the female' is HER, and the 's is simply the verb of 'is embracing'
Prince Albert, Queen Victoria's consort
t is the standard abbreviation for time, and this is the letter thrown away
Princess Diana, known everywhere as Di

annotation.surface: A woman clinging to a prince after squandering hours on a princess and an old sentry.
annotation.walkthrough: Both royals are crossword regulars, Victoria's consort for ALBERT and the Princess of Wales for DI. A halberdier carries a halberd, the axe-headed spear the Vatican's Swiss Guard still parade with.
annotation.definitionFit: A halberdier is a guard carrying a halberd, a weapon four centuries out of date, so 'old guard' names him and puns on the phrase.

entries.clue: Party set up in delightful wood (6)

indicatorNotes.set up: In a down entry, setting something up writes it from the bottom towards the top, so its letters run backwards.
indicatorNotes.in: A thing put in another sits inside it, so these letters go between the letters of the word named next.

blocks.note: dear can mean lovely or delightful, as in 'what a dear little cottage'
a party is a DO, written upwards

annotation.surface: A get-together arranged in a lovely stretch of woodland.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Set up' only reverses in a down entry, which is why the same two words would mean something else across. The deodar is the Himalayan cedar, India's great building timber, and the tree's name and its wood's name are the same word.
annotation.definitionFit: Deodar names both the Himalayan cedar and the close-grained timber cut from it, so 'wood' takes the material sense.

entries.clue: Fool that American sits on (3)

annotation.definitionNote: The second half is a description rather than a synonym: it points at the part of the body, spelt this way only in American English, and has to be read as a whole relative clause.

blocks.note: the donkey standing in for a stupid person, an insult as old as Shakespeare
in American English the word means the backside, where British English says arse

annotation.surface: Some unfortunate being sat on by a visitor from the States.
annotation.walkthrough: The second definition has to be taken as one long phrase, and it defines the thing sat on rather than the sitting. The British spelling of that word has an r in it, which is the whole reason the nationality is specified.
annotation.definitionFit: An ass is a donkey and so a byword for a stupid person, while the same three letters are the American word for the backside, the part anybody sits on.

entries.clue: Had to bring in detectives on street to make critical examination (4,4)

indicatorNotes.to bring in: To bring something in is to bring it inside, so the letters named next are placed within the word before them.
indicatorNotes.on: In a down entry a thing sits on whatever is below it, so the street's letters go underneath — at the end of the answer.

blocks.note: to have a meal is to eat it, so 'had' is ATE, and the word opens after its A
the CID is the Criminal Investigation Department, the branch British plain-clothes detectives belong to
st is the standard abbreviation for street, as on an envelope

annotation.surface: Detectives called in off the street for a thorough grilling.
annotation.walkthrough: The acid test was once literal: nitric acid was dripped on metal because gold alone does not react to it. 'Had' is the meal rather than the possession, and that is the step most solvers reach last.
annotation.definitionFit: An acid test is the trial that settles a matter for good, so it is a critical examination in the sense of the one that actually counts.

entries.clue: The fact of the matter sides denied? A familiar pattern (3)

indicatorNotes.denied: To deny something is to refuse it entry, so the letters named beside it are kept out of the answer.

blocks.note: the truth is what the matter actually amounts to
the letters standing at either side of TRUTH, its first and its last

annotation.surface: Somebody refusing to take sides over what really happened.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sides' means outer letters rather than parties to an argument, and the question mark is the setter flagging the stretch. A rut is the groove wheels wear into a track, which is why it came to mean a routine nobody can climb out of.
annotation.definitionFit: Being in a rut is doing the same thing the same way day after day, so a rut is the pattern that has grown too familiar.

entries.clue: Artist annoying Violet Elizabeth? One with eyes missing nothing (10)

indicatorNotes.missing: Something missing is not there, so the letter it names is taken out of the word before it.

blocks.note: Violet Elizabeth Bott, the lisping child who threatens to 'thcream and thcream' in Richmal Crompton's Just William stories, supplies her surname
the Roman numeral for one
ocelli are the simple eyes of an insect, the small ones set beside the compound pair
nothing is written as O, and that is the letter taken out

annotation.surface: A painter being pestered by a wide-eyed and very noisy little girl.
annotation.walkthrough: Violet Elizabeth Bott is the spoilt child of the Just William books, a fixture of British childhood reading for a century. 'Eyes' wants the entomologist's OCELLI, which is the leap the clue is really asking for.
annotation.definitionFit: Sandro Botticelli painted The Birth of Venus and the Primavera in fifteenth-century Florence, so 'Artist' names him by example.

entries.clue: Non-pay area not operating? Stop suddenly (6)

indicatorNotes.not: 'Not' cancels what comes after it, so those letters are struck out of the word in front.

blocks.note: what costs nothing to have is free
a zone is a marked-off area
a machine that is operating is on, and those are the two letters cancelled

annotation.surface: A corner of town where nobody pays for anything and nothing works.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Non-pay area' reads as a single phrase and has to be broken in the middle for the parse to start. The definition takes the sense the film policeman shouts, not the sense the weather forecast uses.
annotation.definitionFit: To freeze is to stop dead where you stand, the abrupt halt rather than the gradual one.

entries.clue: Troubled medico cares about a fattening drink? (3-5,4)

indicatorNotes.Troubled: Troubled letters are letters in disorder, no longer standing in the order they were handed over in.
indicatorNotes.about: Letters set about a thing close round it, so the single letter following is drawn into the shuffle rather than left outside it.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, eleven letters
the indefinite article taken as the single letter it is, joining the fodder

annotation.surface: A worried doctor fretting over a drink that will do nobody's waistline any good.
annotation.walkthrough: Medico is the informal word for a doctor, and all twelve letters are sitting there before you notice them. An ice-cream soda is soda water with a scoop floating in it, drunk through a straw.
annotation.definitionFit: An ice-cream soda is a drink of soda water with ice cream in it, and the cream and sugar between them earn the 'fattening'.

entries.clue: Deer in pain pursued by leader of louts (5)

indicatorNotes.pursued by: What pursues comes along behind, so the letter it introduces lands at the end of the answer.

blocks.note: a place that hurts is sore
the first letter of louts

annotation.surface: A wounded animal with a young thug close on its heels.
annotation.walkthrough: A sorel is a buck in its third year, one of a whole set of hunting-book words — pricket, sorel, sore — that the old forest manuals left behind and crosswords still keep in work.
annotation.definitionFit: A sorel is a male fallow deer in its third year, so 'Deer' names it by kind rather than as a synonym.

entries.clue: Rather keeping quiet about a principle cheat violates (4,4)

indicatorNotes.keeping: To keep a thing is to hold on to it inside, so the letter named next goes within the word before it.
indicatorNotes.about: To be about something is to be all round it, so what is already assembled closes over the letter that follows.

blocks.note: fairly good and rather good say the same thing
p is piano on a score, the composer's instruction to play softly
the indefinite article taken as the single letter it is

annotation.surface: Somebody saying nothing about a rule that a cheat breaks.
annotation.walkthrough: Two separate insertions go into one word, and the everyday phrase 'keeping quiet about' hides both of them at once. P for quiet is the piano marking on sheet music, not an initial.
annotation.definitionFit: Fair play is the principle that everyone sticks to the rules and nobody takes an unearned advantage, which is precisely what a cheat sets aside.

entries.clue: See 24
Dreadful French art showing fisherman singing? (6)

blocks.note: grim means dreadful, bleak beyond bearing
'art' is the old second-person form of 'to be' — thou art — and the French for that is es

annotation.surface: A bleak piece of French painting with a singing fisherman somewhere in it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'French art' is the clue's best moment: not painting at all but grammar, the thou-form of être. Peter Grimes is the Suffolk fisherman of Britten's 1945 opera, which is why this one sings.
annotation.definitionFit: Peter Grimes, the fisherman at the centre of Britten's opera, is the fisherman who does all his talking in song.

entries.clue: Brawl with soldiers coming out in uncontrolled movement (4,4)

indicatorNotes.coming out: What comes out is taken away, so the letters it names leave the phrase standing in front of them.

blocks.note: a free-for-all is a brawl that anybody may join
OR is Other Ranks, the British Army's term for everybody below commissioned rank

annotation.surface: A mass punch-up that the troops are quietly backing out of.
annotation.walkthrough: OR for soldiers is worth banking: Other Ranks is what the army calls everyone who is not an officer. The two letters come out of the middle of the phrase rather than off either end.
annotation.definitionFit: Free fall is falling under gravity alone with nothing checking the descent, so the movement is uncontrolled in the strictest sense.

entries.clue: Type of building worker, shark with little hesitation (6)

blocks.note: a rigg is the spotted dogfish, a shark small enough to be sold for the fryer
er is the short noise people make while they think of what to say

annotation.surface: A shark that barely pauses before it strikes.
annotation.walkthrough: Rigg is the trade and dialect name for the spotted dogfish, which reaches British chip shops as rock salmon. The hesitation is the noise itself, not an abbreviation of a longer word.
annotation.definitionFit: A rigger erects and maintains the scaffolding, cranes and cradles on a site, so he is one kind of building worker among several.

entries.clue: Religious rite – it is used during illness (7)

indicatorNotes.is used during: What is used during something is used in the middle of it, so these letters go inside the word named next.

blocks.note: the lurgy is British slang for a vague unnamed illness, the thing that is going round
the word it, taken exactly as it stands

annotation.surface: A rite performed at the bedside of somebody who has fallen ill.
annotation.walkthrough: The dreaded lurgy came out of The Goon Show in the 1950s and settled into ordinary British speech for any bug doing the rounds. All but two letters of the answer come from that one slang word.
annotation.definitionFit: A liturgy is the set form of words and actions a church uses for public worship, which is a religious rite laid down in advance.
